steps.action: Authors take up the sea ice pump hypothesis (ikaite precipitation enriching bulk ice in TA relative to TIC) from Rysgaard et al. and the variable TA:TIC ratios reported since.
steps.quote: The sea ice pump was first proposed by Rysgaard et al. (2007)

steps.action: Pose the question of how differing physical and biological processes shape horizontal and vertical carbonate distributions, and whether they alter the single bulk TA and TIC values used in models.
steps.quote: determine if these processes affect the bulk estimates of TA and TIC commonly ingested into models of the sea ice carbon pump

steps.action: Select two level-ice sites 7 km apart, inside and outside an invisible polynya, from Dalman et al. (2019), expecting contrasting currents, ice thickness and algal biomass (a natural laboratory).
steps.quote: we selected two level ice sites (Fig. 1) based on Dalman et al. (2019)

steps.action: Design a statistical sampling scheme (five random cores per site per day on three days, top, middle and bottom 10 cm, n = 15 per horizon) and an ANOVA test of equal site means.
steps.quote: we designed a statistical sampling method in which on each date, five locations were randomly selected

steps.action: Collect under-ice currents, snow depth, ice thickness, temperature and salinity cores, carbonate cores, a high-resolution core and pooled Chl a samples over 6 days in May 2019.
steps.quote: Sampling was conducted over a 6 d period between 4 and 10 May 2019

steps.action: Calibrate the TIC and TA analysers against certified reference material and report precision; replicate each TIC and TA measurement.
steps.quote: Both instruments were calibrated prior to measurement using certified reference material (CRM batch no. 177)

steps.action: Report site conditions: currents an order of magnitude stronger at POLY, ice about 33 cm thinner and snow about 11 cm deeper there, and ice warming over the period.
steps.quote: The polynya site, POLY, experienced considerably higher under-ice currents

steps.action: Compare bottom-ice algal biomass with Dalman et al. (2019) and find it about three times higher at the thick-ice site, the opposite of the earlier result.
steps.quote: In contrast to the results of Dalman et al. (2019), bottom-ice algal biomass was about 3 times higher at TFYI than at POLY

steps.action: Describe the high-resolution TIC, TA and salinity profiles: c-shaped at POLY, a bottom increase only at TFYI, and agreement through most of the ice volume.
steps.quote: The polynya site was characterized by “c-shaped” profiles for TIC, TA, and salinity

steps.action: Use ANOVA to compare the sites by horizon: top higher at POLY, bottom lower at POLY, middle statistically indistinguishable, TA:TIC different only in the bottom.
steps.quote: The middle horizon was statistically indistinguishable between the two sites for all three parameters.

steps.action: Set up rival causes for the thinner polynya ice: enhanced ocean heat flux from strong currents versus deeper snow insulating the ice.
steps.quote: we cannot rule out snow depth as a contributing factor to the invisible polynya

steps.action: Apply thermodynamic-model sensitivity (about 10% thickness change for the observed snow difference, from Flato and Brown) to estimate that snow explains about half of the 20% thickness difference.
steps.quote: it is not unreasonable to estimate that snow may have been responsible for about half of the difference

steps.action: Check that the site snow and ice contrast is not small-scale drifting, using an independent 4.5 km snow and ice transect by a collaborating team.
steps.quote: the long transect conducted on 12 May (Fig. 5) shows a consistent pattern of deeper snow and thin ice

steps.action: Reconstruct freeze-up from AMSR2 sea ice concentration and rule out earlier consolidation (longer snow accumulation) at POLY: both sites consolidated at about the same time.
steps.quote: ice at the two sites consolidated at roughly the same time (Fig. 6)

steps.action: Explain the reversed algal biomass contrast by light limitation under thick polynya snow overriding current-driven nutrient supply; photoacclimation and interannual variability are left open.
steps.quote: it is most likely that light limitation under thick snow at the polynya site overshadowed any potential boost in production from current-driven nutrient supply

steps.action: State rivals for higher top-horizon salinity at POLY: faster initial growth, turbulent frazil-favouring formation, and early-season flooding.
steps.quote: another explanation is that ice formation at the two sites occurred under different turbulence conditions

steps.action: Compare the salinity standard deviation with the Weeks and Lee (1962) thresholds; higher variability at POLY supports the turbulence explanation.
steps.quote: the standard deviation of salinity we observed was indeed much higher at the polynya site (1.2) than the thick first-year ice site (0.4)

steps.action: Derive the expectation of conservative brine rejection: a mixing line between pure ice and a seawater endmember averaged from the authors' summer 2016-2019 station R3 samples.
steps.quote: if sea ice carbonate chemistry were only impacted by brine rejection, we would expect bulk TIC and TA to be higher

steps.action: Compare samples with the mixing line: middle and bottom follow it, while top samples fall well below it for both TIC and TA at both sites.
steps.quote: the top core sections are substantially lower (for both TIC and TA) than the mixing line

steps.action: Reject ikaite precipitation alone as the cause of the top depletion, because TIC was depleted about twice as much as TA; favour CO2 gas evasion, with ikaite as a secondary contributor.
steps.quote: precipitation alone would result in TA being twice as depleted as TIC, and what we observed is the opposite

steps.action: From the growth-rate-salinity relation and the Feltham et al. (2002) current-driven drainage prediction, expect lower middle-horizon salinity, TA and TIC at the polynya.
steps.quote: We therefore anticipated lower salinity and perhaps lower TA and TIC in the polynya ice

steps.action: Test the expectation with ANOVA: there is no significant middle-horizon difference, so the expectation fails.
steps.quote: Table 3 shows that our expectations were not met

steps.action: Revise the account: estimated mid-winter growth rates (about 0.6 versus 0.7 cm per day) differ too little between sites to produce salinity or carbonate differences.
steps.quote: the small differences in growth rates between the two sites were not enough to produce noticeable differences in salinity, nor in TIC or TA

steps.action: Exclude biological drawdown as the main driver of bottom-horizon differences: higher TIC and TA at the high-Chl a site follow salinity and the mixing line.
steps.quote: physical processes (brine rejection) and not biological processes (i.e., the ice algae bloom) were most responsible for carbonate system differences

steps.action: Check with salinity-normalized nTA versus nTIC regressions against process slopes; no horizon follows the photosynthesis line, and bottom slopes shift toward net respiration, consistent with Campbell et al.
steps.quote: To further check for the impact of primary production on the bottom ice horizon

steps.action: Ask whether ikaite precipitation is apparent or important in the samples.
steps.quote: So, is ikaite precipitation apparent (or important) in our samples?

steps.action: Compare TA:TIC ratios (about 1.05 below the surface) with the seawater ratio and with Rysgaard et al.'s ratios near 2:1; they match most later studies near 1:1.
steps.quote: not meaningfully different from our estimate of the source seawater TA : TIC ratio (1.04)

steps.action: Keep the claim that ikaite precipitates (nTA-nTIC slopes of 0.5-1.0 in all horizons) but too little, or is lost with brine, to fractionate TA and TIC substantially.
steps.quote: ikaite precipitation certainly seems to be occurring in our study area

steps.action: Compute vertically weighted mean TIC, TA and TA:TIC per site; differences are 2.6%, 4.6% and 2.0%.
steps.quote: when a weighted vertical average of the two sites is calculated, the carbonate chemistry (particularly the TA : TIC ratio) is not meaningfully different

steps.action: Conclude that brine drainage dominates sea ice carbonate chemistry over gas evasion, respiration and ikaite, so bulk values may be predicted empirically from salinity and source seawater.
steps.quote: these processes were dominated by brine drainage processes as evidenced by strong relationships with salinity

tree.answer: Variability of sea ice TIC, TA and TA:TIC between studies and sites, contrasted across an invisible polynya
Partly: TIC, TA, salinity and Chl a are measured directly; process contributions are inferred from mixing lines and normalized slopes
Characterize process controls on carbonate distributions and test whether they change the bulk values used in models
Brine rejection, ikaite precipitation, gas evasion, biology; for salinity: growth rate, turbulence or frazil, flooding; for ice thickness: heat flux versus snow
Yes: distinct nTA/nTIC slopes (17/106, 2/1, 1/1) and a conservative mixing line
Conditions found: a natural spatial contrast between polynya and thick-ice sites, not set

tree.question: 6b
tree.answer: Only weakly: one season, two sites, three sampling days with 15 cores per horizon
Partly: statistical sampling confirms the high-resolution core patterns; an independent transect; a normalization check; the middle-horizon expectation failed and the account was revised
Best explanation: brine drainage dominates, and vertically averaged chemistry is similar despite contrasting conditions
No review file supplied; reviewers are named only in the acknowledgements

end.claim: Despite strongly contrasting physical and biological conditions, site differences in sea ice carbonate chemistry were confined to thin top and bottom layers, vertically averaged TIC, TA and TA:TIC were not meaningfully different, and brine drainage (salinity) rather than gas evasion, respiration or ikaite dominated the distributions.

decisive_move.sentence: The statistical sampling design (15 random cores per horizon per site, tested with ANOVA) is what allowed the authors to claim statistically indistinguishable middle horizons and similar bulk chemistry despite sea ice heterogeneity.

gates.evidence: Site selection followed the expected contrast from Dalman et al. (2019) (§2.1 ¶2), and the sampling and ANOVA design was fixed to test site differences (§2.2 ¶4). The middle-horizon expectation of lower salinity at the polynya could fail and did fail (§4.3 ¶1). No hypothesis or analysis was preregistered, and the explicit expectations appear only in the Discussion.

imports.item: Analysis of variance (ANOVA) for between-site mean differences
Modified Gran titration for total alkalinity
Infrared gas analyzer (LI-COR LI-7000) for CO2 released by acid extraction
Acetone-extraction fluorometry for Chl a (Holm-Hansen equations)
Commercial meat vacuum sealer for gas-tight sample bags
Guides' knowledge of prevailing northeast winds

novelty_claims.quote: To our knowledge, the present study is the first attempt to employ a statistical sampling approach to compare sea ice carbonate chemistry between two sites.
ice texture (e.g., frazil vs. congelation ice) may have an impact on CO 2 release potential, but to our knowledge this has not been investigated

limits: Sub-claims at other statuses: the site differences in top and bottom horizons and the middle-horizon similarity are tested by ANOVA (closest to confirmed as observational differences); ikaite occurring with little effect is best_explanation; snow explaining about half the thickness difference is estimate_with_resolution, without stated uncertainty; light limitation of algae is best_explanation, with photoacclimation and interannual variability left open; frazil texture and flooding are not tested (no thin sections). Design limits: one season (May 2019), two sites, three days; Chl a n = 3 per site; no under-ice seawater, so the endmember comes from summer samples (n = 5); no direct ikaite identification. Many ANOVA tests are run at p < 0.01 with no stated multiple-comparison correction. The supplement (Figs. S1, S2) was not supplied. No review file was supplied, although reviewers are named, so no review sequence is coded. Inference: whether the Discussion expectations (e.g., the middle horizon) were formed before the data were seen cannot be determined from the text.

disagreements.target: Dalman et al. (2019): higher bottom-ice algal biomass in the polynya
disagreements.support: Pooled bottom-ice Chl a samples on three dates, plus visible algae in essentially all cores, show about 3 times more biomass at the thick-ice site; this is attributed to snow light limitation.
disagreements.quote: In contrast to the results of Dalman et al. (2019), bottom-ice algal biomass was about 3 times higher at TFYI than at POLY

disagreements.target: Rysgaard et al. (2007): bulk sea ice TA:TIC ratios approaching 2:1 as evidence of the sea ice pump
disagreements.support: Middle and bottom TA:TIC ratios are about 1.05, close to the seawater ratio of 1.04, in line with most later studies.
disagreements.quote: [...] formulation of the sea ice pump hypothesis (Rysgaard et al., 2007) reported bulk TA : TIC ratios approaching 2 : 1

disagreements.target: Community position that spatial heterogeneity explains divergent sea ice carbonate results between studies
disagreements.support: Two sites at extremes of spatial variability give similar vertically averaged chemistry (Table 5), so other factors, perhaps methodologies, are suggested.
disagreements.quote: suggests that we should perhaps be looking at other factors (perhaps methodologies) to explain divergent reports of sea ice carbonate chemistry

disagreements.target: Past studies attributing low bottom-ice TIC to algal biological drawdown (Brown et al., 2015; Delille et al., 2007)
disagreements.support: Higher TIC at the higher-Chl a site follows salinity and the mixing line, and normalized slopes do not follow the photosynthesis line.
disagreements.quote: This counterintuitive result is explained again by salinity

disagreements.target: Expected growth-rate control of bulk salinity (Cox and Weeks, 1975; Vancoppenolle et al., 2006) and current-driven drainage (Feltham et al., 2002)
disagreements.support: No significant middle-horizon difference in salinity, TA or TIC between sites with different growth rates and currents.
disagreements.quote: Table 3 shows that our expectations were not met

disagreements.target: Modelling studies prescribing a single TA:TIC ratio of about 2:1 (Rysgaard et al., 2011; Grimm et al., 2016; Mortenson et al., 2018)
disagreements.support: A single bulk value per parameter is justified at coarse resolution, but the measured ratio is near 1:1 and likely varies by region with source water and salinity.
disagreements.quote: Exactly what value to use (particularly for the TIC : TA ratio) likely varies by region

alternatives_considered.chosen: Statistical sampling of 15 cores per horizon per site
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Single high-resolution cores compared between sites
alternatives_considered.reason: Inherent heterogeneity of sea ice makes it difficult to compare single samples quantitatively (Miller et al., 2015)

alternatives_considered.chosen: Seawater endmember from summer below-halocline samples at station R3, 2016-2019
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Under-ice seawater samples, as used in past studies
alternatives_considered.reason: Under-ice seawater samples were not collected during the study

alternatives_considered.chosen: Normalization nX = Xmeas/Smeas × Sref (Friis et al., 2003)
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Normalizations for systems with a nonzero zero-salinity endmember (implied)
alternatives_considered.reason: Appropriate where the S = 0 endmember has TA and TIC equal to 0, as for pure ice

alternatives_considered.chosen: Different turbulence regimes (frazil production) for higher top salinity at POLY
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Faster initial growth rate; early-season flooding under deeper snow
alternatives_considered.reason: Higher salinity standard deviation at POLY matches turbulent-growth variability (Weeks and Lee, 1962; Weeks, 2010)

alternatives_considered.chosen: CO2 gas evasion as the primary cause of top-horizon depletion, ikaite secondary
alternatives_considered.reason: Ikaite alone would deplete TA twice as much as TIC; the opposite was observed

alternatives_considered.chosen: Ocean heat flux plus snow (about half) for the thinner polynya ice
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Snow depth alone; small-scale drifting; earlier ice consolidation
alternatives_considered.reason: Thermodynamic models give about 10% for the snow difference; the transect shows a consistent pattern; AMSR2 shows the same consolidation timing

alternatives_considered.chosen: Light limitation under thick snow for lower polynya algal biomass
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Current-driven nutrient boost; photoacclimation; interannual variability
alternatives_considered.reason: Snow depth is the dominant limiting factor in early spring, and snow over 25 cm limits accumulation (Leu et al., 2015)
